title: Gandhi and the Homeopath: Can a Sick Doctor Heal?
summary: When a homeopathic doctor mentioned that his chief medical officer was bedridden with fever, Gandhi quipped: 'If the doctor himself falls sick, how can patients respect him? I did not inherit stomach bugs from my ancestors!'
keywords: Gandhi and the Homeopath: Can a Sick Doctor Heal?
Mahatma Gandhi & Dr. B. C. Roy
full_text:
In 1932, Mahatma Gandhi was conducting rigorous dietary and lifestyle experiments in his ashram, advocating for natural hygiene, fresh air, and mindful eating.

A homeopathic physician arrived to examine Gandhi's health and offer medical counsel.

During their conversation, the doctor proudly remarked:
"Gandhiji! We have a brilliant senior medical director in our association. He is an extraordinary scholar. However, for the past two weeks, he has been bedridden with severe fever and stomach distress, being treated as my patient!"

Gandhi adjusted his spectacles, his eyes twinkling:
"What is this I hear? A doctor lying sick in bed as a patient?
My dear doctor! If a physician who preaches health to the world cannot govern his own bodily appetites and lies in bed, how can the public place their trust in him? Shouldn't a doctor be an exemplar of health rather than a casualty of disease?"

The doctor attempted to defend his colleague: "Gandhiji! When seasons change, anyone can succumb to viral infections. Besides, certain physical weaknesses are inherited from parents, are they not?"

Gandhi replied with sharp, playful wit:
"Is that so? Well, I certainly did not inherit tapeworms or dysentery microbes from my ancestors as ancestral property! Clean food, self-restraint, and daily exercise keep infections at bay!"

Sitting nearby, Gandhi's close confidant Dr. B. C. Roy (the legendary physician and later Chief Minister of West Bengal) burst into laughter.

The visiting doctor then presented his personality notes on Gandhi: "I have written here: 'Intellectually brilliant, deeply modest, spiritual philosopher.' Is this accurate, Gandhiji?"

Gandhi shrugged: "How on earth should I know?"

Dr. B. C. Roy chimed in with a grin: "Doctor, add one more vital trait: 'Whenever anyone accuses him of virtue, he immediately disputes the charge in court!'"

The doctor protested: "But that is what I meant by modesty!"

Gandhi retorted instantly: "I have never claimed that modesty was my strong suit!"

The room dissolved into hearty laughter, leaving behind Gandhi's timeless lesson: those who teach virtue and health must first live it in their own flesh and blood.
moral: Beyond the humor lies Gandhi's core ethical conviction: teachers, physicians, and politicians must embody their own teachings before preaching to the public.
